title: Muscles of the upper back in layers: trapezius, rhomboids, and levator scapulae (posterior)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender, with surface detail added by an image model.

rows: Medial third of the superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae, and the spinous processes of C7 to T12.
Lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion, and the spine of the scapula.
Accessory nerve (CN XI) for movement. C3 and C4 carry pain and proprioception.
Upper fibers raise the scapula, middle fibers retract it, and lower fibers depress it. Upper and lower fibers together rotate the scapula upward.
hy: Injury to the accessory nerve, for example during surgery in the posterior triangle of the neck, causes a drooping shoulder and weakness raising the arm above the horizontal.

rows: Transverse processes of C1 to C4.
Medial border of the scapula, from the superior angle to the root of the spine.
Dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and branches of C3 and C4.
Raises the scapula and turns its glenoid cavity downward. With the scapula fixed, bends the neck to its own side.
Lower part of the nuchal ligament and the spinous processes of C7 and T1.
Medial border of the scapula at the root of the spine of the scapula.
Retracts the scapula and rotates it so that the glenoid cavity faces downward. It also helps hold the scapula against the thoracic wall.
Spinous processes of T2 to T5.
Medial border of the scapula, from the root of the spine of the scapula to the inferior angle.
Retracts the scapula and rotates it so that the glenoid cavity faces downward. It also helps hold the scapula against the thoracic wall.
Lower part of the ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7 to T3.
Upper borders of ribs 2 to 5, lateral to their angles.
Raises ribs 2 to 5. It is traditionally called a muscle of inspiration, but its real role may be mostly proprioceptive.
Lower half of the ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7 to T3.
Mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral third of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone.
Posterior rami of cervical spinal nerves.
Both sides together extend the head and neck. One side alone bends the head to that side and turns the face to the same side.
Spinous processes of T3 to T6.
Transverse processes of C1 to C3.
Posterior rami of cervical spinal nerves.
Both sides together extend the neck. One side alone bends the neck to that side and turns it to the same side.
Superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.

Starts abduction of the arm, where it is the main abductor for about the first 15 degrees, and then helps the deltoid through the rest of the movement. Holds the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity.
hy: The most often injured rotator cuff muscle: its tendon is pinched under the acromion. Tested with the empty can (Jobe) test.
Rotator cuff muscles, SItS: Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, teres minor, Subscapularis.

rows: Middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
Laterally rotates the arm. Holds the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity.
Upper two thirds of the lateral border of the scapula, on its posterior surface.
Inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
Laterally rotates the arm. Holds the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity.
Posterior surface of the inferior angle of the scapula.
Medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.
Adducts and medially rotates the arm. Helps extend it from a flexed position.
Flat triangular bone on the back of the chest wall, over ribs 2 to 7.
Head of the humerus at the glenoid cavity and the clavicle at the acromion.
Spine, acromion, coracoid process, glenoid cavity, suprascapular notch, and the supraspinous, infraspinous, and subscapular fossae.
hy: When serratus anterior is paralyzed by injury to the long thoracic nerve, the medial border of the scapula lifts off the chest wall (winged scapula).

rows: S-shaped bone that lies horizontally at the root of the neck and connects the upper limb to the trunk.
Manubrium of the sternum at its medial end and the acromion of the scapula at its lateral end.
The medial two-thirds are convex forward and the lateral third is flattened. Conoid tubercle and trapezoid line for the coracoclavicular ligament.
hy: One of the most often fractured bones, usually in its middle third. Its weakest point is where the middle and lateral thirds meet. Sternocleidomastoid pulls the medial piece up and the weight of the arm drags the lateral piece down.

rows: Glenoid cavity of the scapula above, and the radius and the ulna at the elbow.
Head, anatomical and surgical necks, greater and lesser tubercles, deltoid tuberosity, radial groove, capitulum, trochlea, medial and lateral epicondyles.
hy: Three nerves lie against the bone and are injured by fractures at those sites: the axillary nerve at the surgical neck, the radial nerve in the radial groove at midshaft, and the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.
A supracondylar fracture, common in children, threatens the brachial artery and the median nerve.

rows: Back and base of the skull.
Parietal bones at the lambdoid suture, the temporal bones, the sphenoid, and the atlas (C1) at the occipital condyles.
Foramen magnum, occipital condyles, hypoglossal canals, and the external occipital protuberance.
hy: The foramen magnum transmits the lower end of the brainstem, the vertebral arteries, and the spinal roots of the accessory nerve. The hypoglossal canal transmits CN XII.

rows: The seven vertebrae of the neck.

Small bodies. Each transverse process has a transverse foramen, which carries the vertebral artery in C1 to C6. The spinous processes of C2 to C6 are forked. The atlas (C1) has no body, the axis (C2) has the dens, and C7 has a long spinous process that can be felt.
hy: There are eight cervical spinal nerves for seven vertebrae: C1 to C7 leave above the vertebra of the same number and C8 leaves below C7.
Instability of the joint between the atlas and the dens occurs in rheumatoid arthritis and in Down syndrome and can compress the spinal cord.

rows: The twelve vertebrae of the chest. Each carries a pair of ribs.
Facets for the ribs on the bodies and on most transverse processes, heart-shaped bodies, and long spinous processes that slope downward.
